units.text: Dana rolls the dice again. On the map, a tiny army blocks her access to a continent. She calculated reasonably. She lost unreasonably. Her friends laugh, and she declares, with the authority of a general who answers to no history, that the next attack will put things right.

In another room, Andrei watches a coding agent. It has modified twenty files, run some tests, and announced that the problem is solved. The application starts. The main button works. Then a user with a different permission appears, and everything gets tangled. Andrei writes: “Check again. We are very close.”

Mara is looking at neither a map nor code. Her conversation is already the length of a book. It began with an intuition about memory and meaning. The model found analogies, proposed a vocabulary, built an architecture, and suggested that the perspective might open an important direction. Mara now has a title for her theory. She does not yet have an experiment that distinguishes it from alternatives.
All three say almost the same thing: one more.

None of these scenes proves that anyone has a problem. Dana is enjoying herself. Andrei may be one step away from a useful repair. Mara may have a fertile intuition that is not yet adequately formulated. An observer who automatically condemned continuing would miss precisely the mechanism that makes games, engineering, and research interesting.

But that same observer would also be wrong to declare that every new attempt means progress. Sometimes the next version preserves what we have learned. At other times, it changes the scenery and sells us the original hope all over again.

At a gaming table, the rules tell us relatively clearly what winning means. In a conversation about a big idea, the prize is less well defined. It may be a proof. It may be a magnificent sentence. It may be the conviction that someone finally understands us. And if these prizes become confused, users can leave happy without having obtained what they came looking for.
This is the book’s problem: not the mere existence of chance, but the difficulty of recognizing a gain.

We will begin by defending surprise. A completely predictable life would not necessarily be a good life. Then we will explore how a machine that produces language can also produce confidence, dependence on affirmation, or, in certain contexts, the aggravation of clinical vulnerabilities. We will enter offices where tools become faster but days do not become shorter. Finally, we will build a way out that does not involve discarding technology: a way of connecting results to evidence without pretending that every human question can be reduced to an automated test.
The point is not never to say “one more try” again. The point is to know what exactly we are trying.
PART I The Pleasure of an Open Future
